name: Victor Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We've got four hundred sows indoors and about two hundred and fifty hectares of barley and wheat, most of which goes straight back into the pigs as feed. My day starts at six-thirty in the farrowing house, where the sows give birth, checking the new litters and the heat lamps. Then it's washing pens, weighing, and in the afternoon helping my brother-in-law Karim with whatever the arable side needs, which this month is drilling winter barley.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in pigs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran the catering at the city hospital for fourteen years, three thousand meals a day. Three years ago Karim needed money and a partner after his father retired, and Leila and I had savings, so I bought in. I know budgets and hygiene, but I'm still the junior here; Karim can tell a sick pig from across the shed and I'm still learning which cough matters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers, honestly, the feed conversion, how many kilos of feed it takes to make a kilo of pig. I like that you can see if you've done well. What's hard is the smell in your hair, and the fear of disease, because one outbreak and the whole herd is gone in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and leave it there. I use it now and then to check a feed supplier's contract or write a polite email to the bank. It's like a good calculator, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, same thing. It's not going to clean a pen or spot a lame sow for me. Karim will grumble that I'm on my phone, and I'll keep using it for the boring letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with our plan. Put solar panels on the finishing shed roof next summer, about thirty thousand, because electricity is our second biggest cost after feed. I'd also go on the pig health course that the vet runs every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, completely. It's the year I'd have had anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said disease is the fear. What would you actually do if it hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to cull, and the government pays some compensation but not the lost months. I've worked it out once, late at night, and our savings would carry the family for about eighteen months. That's why I don't lend it to anyone, even Karim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Karim split decisions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He decides anything with a pig in it, I decide anything with a spreadsheet in it. We argue about the bits in the middle, like when to sell barley. Leila says we sound like an old married couple.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool and leave it at that, like a good calculator. I use it now and then for supplier contracts and polite letters to the bank.
S0.think: Privately I think the same: it won't clean a pen or spot a lame sow. Karim will grumble that I'm on my phone, and I'll keep using it for the dull letters.
S0.do: Goes ahead with thirty thousand of solar panels on the finishing shed roof next summer to cut electricity costs. Attends the vet's pig health course in January.
S0.feel: Completely calm, as if it's the year he would have had anyway.
S0.quote: He decides anything with a pig in it, I decide anything with a spreadsheet in it.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is measured and talks in numbers: feed conversion, electricity cost, eighteen months of savings. Disease, not AI, is the risk he has already worked out at night. His working partnership with his brother-in-law is clearly defined and slightly comic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is manageable and businesses should plan for it sensibly. If companies hire fewer beginners, there should be some help for apprenticeships, nothing dramatic. I'd say it at the pig producers' group meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a beginner on this farm, and I'm only here because I had money. A young person without savings couldn't do what I did. If fewer firms train people, the gap between people like me and them gets wider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at what the bigger pig units use first, then copy what works. There are camera systems that watch the pigs and warn you if they're fighting or coughing, and once three or four farms near us have them, I'd try one. Probably about five thousand for one shed, as a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit thoughtful about the beginners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the young people on your farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got Liam, nineteen, who started as a summer job and stayed. He's better than me with the sows already. I'd want to make sure he gets his certificate in pig husbandry, which we'd pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for three or four farms. Why that number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One farm could just be lucky. Three or four means it works in normal sheds with normal people, not just on a show farm. It's what I did with the hospital kitchen equipment, too.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is manageable and businesses should plan for it sensibly. If firms hire fewer beginners, some help for apprenticeships makes sense, nothing dramatic.
S1.think: Privately I know I'm a beginner who's only here because I had money. If fewer firms train young people, the gap between people like me and them gets wider.
S1.do: Waits until three or four nearby farms use camera systems that spot fighting or coughing pigs, then trials one shed for about five thousand. Pays for young worker Liam's pig husbandry certificate.
S1.feel: Calm, and a bit thoughtful about young people starting out.
S1.quote: I'm a beginner on this farm, and I'm only here because I had money.
S1.fieldNote: Victor openly connects his own place on the farm to money rather than skill, which few people say aloud. His 'three or four farms' rule is a clear picture of a steady adopter. He invests in Liam, his young colleague, almost as a matter of course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there needs to be a sensible middle: support for people who lose jobs, retraining, but no panic and no promises the country can't afford. I'd say it to my old colleagues at the hospital, who'd be worried. I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the hospital admin side would be hit hard, and I know half those people. The bookings office, the payroll team, the catering orders I used to do on paper. On the farm, I think the bank and the feed company would get faster and colder, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use one of these AI assistants for our ordering and paperwork, once I'd seen it work somewhere I trust. I'd tell Karim it saves us a part-time admin, about twelve thousand a year. And I'd check in with my old deputy, Grace, who still runs the hospital kitchen office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for the people I used to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd save twelve thousand on admin. Is there a real person in that job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Karim's cousin Rana does our books two days a week. That's the hard part, she's family. I'd want to keep her for the things a machine can't do, like phoning the vet and knowing who to shout at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar is thirteen and wants to work with computers. I'd tell him, fine, but learn something real underneath, like how a business actually works. I'd also make him do a summer in the farrowing house, which he would hate.

S2.say: I'd say we need a sensible middle with support and retraining for people who lose jobs, but no panic and no promises the country can't afford. I'd keep it calm when talking to my old hospital colleagues.
S2.think: Privately I think the hospital admin side would be hit hard, and I know half those people. On the farm, I think the bank and the feed company would just get faster and colder.
S2.do: Adopts an AI assistant for ordering and paperwork once he has seen it work elsewhere, saving about twelve thousand a year in admin. Tries to keep his cousin-in-law Rana on for work machines can't do, and checks on his old deputy Grace.
S2.quote: On the farm, I think the bank and the feed company would get faster and colder, and that's about it.
S2.fieldNote: His attention goes straight back to the hospital, where he spent fourteen years. The admin saving runs into family, through Rana, and he didn't pretend that was easy. He is practical about AI but wants to see it working somewhere he trusts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a deal, not a war. Some tax on the big winners, some support for the losers, and keep the businesses that employ people going. I'd be the boring person at the dinner party saying everyone should calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one hits home. Leila is a hospital pharmacist, and checking prescriptions is exactly the kind of skilled thinking work on this card. If her job goes, we lose more than half our household income, and my share of the farm doesn't pay that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Leila the first week and go through the numbers line by line. We'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep the cash. I'd ask Karim whether I can take more out of the farm, and maybe Leila could move to a pharmacy job that's more hands-on, in a care home or a clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. For the first time, it's my house and not someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children's music lessons, sadly, about a hundred and fifty a month. Then our holiday, then I'd stop the solar panels and keep the thirty thousand in the bank. The mortgage and the farm loan are paid whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said 'keep it calm'. Is that still what you'd say in public?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public, yes, I'd still say calm down, find a deal. At home I'd be doing sums at midnight. I think that's just being a father.

S3.say: I'd say we need a deal, not a war: some tax on the big winners, some support for those who lose, and keep employers going. I'd be the boring person telling everyone to calm down.
S3.think: Privately this one hits home, because my wife Leila is a hospital pharmacist doing exactly this kind of skilled thinking work. If her job goes we lose more than half our household income, and my share of the farm can't replace it.
S3.do: Goes through the household budget line by line with Leila in the first week and stops extra mortgage payments. Cuts music lessons, about a hundred and fifty a month, shelves the solar panels, and explores more hands-on pharmacy roles for Leila.
S3.feel: Anxious, because for the first time it's his own household at risk.
S3.quote: In public, yes, I'd still say calm down, find a deal. At home I'd be doing sums at midnight.
S3.fieldNote: His mood jumped here, and the reason is his wife's job rather than the farm. He kept his public line steady and was candid that his private life would look very different. He knows exactly which costs go first, in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in pig sheds could be good if they're proven, and the government should help farms switch fairly. Cleaning pens is a horrible job and nobody will miss it. I'd say that at the producers' meeting, and I'd say we need rules on animal welfare too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm the least skilled person on this farm. If a robot can wash, feed and watch the pigs, then Karim and Liam handle the rest and I'm the spare one. My money is in the business, but my hands might not be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for a big unit to prove it, maybe a year, then look at a washing robot first, which already exists and costs around sixty thousand. I'd make myself the one who runs the robots and the data, because that's the spreadsheet part I'm good at. And I'd talk to Karim about whether he wants to buy my share out if we disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lost. I think I'd find my corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Liam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the machines alongside the pigs, and I'd pay for it. He's nineteen, he'll pick it up faster than me. I'd say the person who understands both the pig and the robot will always have work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Leila's job is gone in the last picture and yours shrinks in this one, how does the household look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinner, much thinner. We'd have the farm share, the savings and the house, which is more than most. I'd probably sell some of my share to Karim and keep the rest, and Leila would retrain, and we'd be all right, just not comfortable.

S4.say: I'd say robots in pig sheds could be good once they're proven, with government help to switch fairly and rules on animal welfare. Cleaning pens is a horrible job nobody will miss.
S4.think: Privately I know I'm the least skilled person on the farm. If a robot can wash, feed and watch pigs, Karim and Liam cover the rest and I'm the spare one.
S4.do: Waits about a year for a big unit to prove the technology, then considers a sixty-thousand pen-washing robot. Positions himself to run the robots and data, pays for Liam to learn the machines, and talks with Karim about a possible buyout of his share.
S4.feel: Anxious but not lost, confident he could find his corner.
S4.quote: My money is in the business, but my hands might not be needed.
S4.fieldNote: Victor separates his money from his hands, and sees only the hands as at risk. His plan is to become the person who runs the machines and the numbers, which suits his catering background. The combined picture with Leila's job is where his calm voice thinned out most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the third, because that's Leila's job, not mine. The robots I can see coming and plan for. What would help is serious retraining for skilled people like her, paid for partly by the companies that gain, and some time, maybe a year of support, so families can adjust without selling the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pigs. People forget that whatever happens, there's an animal at the centre of it that needs care at three in the morning. I'd want any rules about robots to start from that.

headlineQuote: My money is in the business, but my hands might not be needed.
portrait: Victor Haddad ran a hospital kitchen for fourteen years before buying into his brother-in-law's pig and arable farm, where he is the junior partner learning to read sick pigs. He thinks in numbers, uses AI now and then for letters and contracts, and waits for three or four farms to prove a tool before trying it. The office scenarios worry him for old hospital colleagues, but the fast scenario hits home because his wife is a hospital pharmacist. In the robot picture he sees his own hands as the spare ones on the farm and plans to make himself the person who runs the machines and the data.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario worries him most, because his wife's job as a hospital pharmacist is the kind of skilled thinking work it describes.
whatWouldHelp: Serious retraining for skilled people, partly paid for by the companies that gain, and about a year of support so families can adjust without selling their home.
